rv.q: ‘The Portuguese Kid,” John Patrick Shanley’s latest play, is the funniest new comedy I’ve reviewed since…well, maybe ever.
The play is piffle, but you will laugh in spite of yourself.

Part farce, part rom-com, the occasionally funny but ultimately trivial play moves from run-of-the mill law office to Barry’s beach house, to Atalanta’s blue-on-blue bedroom and overly ornate backyard (sets by John Lee Beatty), but doesn’t really go anywhere that’s not completely predictable.
The play is all talk, none of it amusing or interesting, even in the hands of capable supporting players like Aimee Carrero as Barry's bimbo wife and Pico Alexander as Atalanta's jailbait boyfriend.
Despite their ingenuity, the 100-minute play moves like a kicked horse: fast but grudging.
But The Portuguese Kid's ideas about passion and gender are shot through with retrograde banality.
The Portuguese Kid has about as much objective as an episode of Keeping Up With the Kardashians and an arc that’s equal parts lazy predictability and seriously unfunny topicality.
You will laugh — of that I have no doubt!
Of course, in a romantic comedy, the journey matters more than the destination — and with a cast full of scene-stealing actors like Kid’s, that journey is an uproariously entertaining one.
But happily Scott and Alexander turn every rough diamond into a polished gem.

The Portuguese Kid isn't a great play, and it's certainly not on par with Shanley's two most substantial works, the ethics drama Doubt and the rom-com Moonstruck. But it's definitely a crowd pleaser...

But operating here also as a director, Shanley manages to massage this on-paper mishmash with capable actors and the smartest production values Manhattan Theatre Club can buy, and the result is one hundred minutes of agreeable, albeit fitful, amusement.

A few days after attending the production, I made a point of reading through the script and found it a slight but cute and well-meaning romance, which makes me suspect that the play may fare better under a different director who does not encourage oversized performances.
In fairness, Shanley cooks up some zesty zingers, and the cast serves them nicely.
"The Portuguese Kid" is as predictable as it is old-fashioned – a hoary pseudo-romantic comedy trafficking in insulting stereotypes that died well before Don Rickles did.
But where the heart ought to be there's nothing but the shifting gears of a playwright pushing characters into outlandish situations that are rarely amusing.

The Portuguese Kid has it all: idiosyncratic characters you cannot help but champion, rambunctious dialogue that leaves you occasionally breathless, and a director’s deft massage of the actors’ already polished gifts for comic timing.
Shanley’s feel-good romp is undoubtedly an enjoyable night out, presenting a poignant commentary on how we treat our world, how we treat each other, and ultimately, how we treat ourselves.
Scott plies her au natural comic abilities to perfection.
"Gather a cast of first-class actors, add some laughs, some romance and chances are, you have a pretty good play.
It’s a playful luncheon, but one that leaves you half-full dining on mediocre fish, and only enjoyable if you’ve had a few strong drinks.
John Patrick Shanley’s The Portuguese Kid has some great acting and some rather funny dialogue, but it is short on substance.

Overall, though Shanley's "The Portuguese Kid" attempts to be a hilarious battle of the sexes, its laughs are shallow and simplistic and, unfortunately, rewarding of views that don't quite sit right with our current politics.
In The Portuguese Kid, Shanley most certainly does not underestimate women — or his audience.
The Portuguese Kid is old hat, its jokes are uninspired, and it's all too overstated and laugh-hungry.

cn.t: Critics are divided on Shanley's broad romantic comedy, with some finding laughs in Alexander and Scott's chemistry while others dismiss it as a tired, substance-free retread of "Moonstruck" with strained humor and weak plotting.
